claim: SARS-CoV-2 spike protein candidate adaptive polymorphisms (CAPs) were identified using evolutionary probability (EP) approach with a threshold of EP < 0.05.
source: Residues with an EP < 0.05 in the target sequence are candidate adaptive polymorphisms (CAPs) (red). CAPs are found at sites 32, 50, 218, 346, 372, 478, 486, 498, 519, 604, 681, 682, 683, 684, and 1125.
evidence: The manuscript describes the computational method used to identify CAPs and provides specific site numbers. Figure 1A-B shows the EP distribution and CAP locations.

claim: CAPs are found at sites 32, 50, 218, 346, 372, 478, 486, 498, 519, 604, 681, 682, 683, 684, and 1125 in the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein.
evidence: Direct statement of specific residue positions identified as CAPs through EP analysis.

claim: A majority of CAP positions reside at the receptor-binding domain (RBD) and the Furin cleavage site.
source: We observe that a majority of the CAP positions reside at the receptor-binding domain (RBD) and the Furin cleavage site (676-689; Wrobel et al., 2020) shown as transparent light gray spheres.
evidence: Statement supported by Figure 1C showing CAP locations on the protein structure.

claim: There is an overlap between identified CAPs and mutations suggested by other methods to be adaptive for the S protein.
source: Indeed, there is an overlap between these CAPs and the mutations suggested by other methods to be adaptive for the S protein (Cagliani et al., 2020; Singh and Yi, 2021; Kistler et al., 2022; Starr et al., 2022b).
evidence: Comparison with published literature showing agreement between methods.

claim: Sites 478, 486, 498, and 681 have been implicated in SARS-CoV-2 evolution by other studies.
source: Within these studies, sites 478, 486, 498, and 681 have been implicated in SARS-CoV-2 evolution, leaving the remaining 11 CAPs as undiscovered candidate sites for adaptation.
evidence: Reference to prior studies identifying specific sites as important for evolution.

claim: The Furin cleavage site plays a key role in the opening process of the S protein.
source: The Furin cleavage site plays a key role in the opening process as the binding of host cell protease Furin aids in the cleavage of the S protein into two domains: S1 and S2 (Wrobel et al., 2020: 13).
evidence: Statement about functional role supported by citation.

claim: CAPs in closed chains have negative coupling asymmetry with respect to the hACE2 binding site interface in the RBD-open chain.
source: In support of these findings, we observe through DCIasym that when the S protein is in its pre-fusion conformation with one chain open, the CAPs in the closed chains have negative coupling asymmetry with respect to the hACE2 binding site interface in the RBD-open chain.
evidence: DCIasym analysis results shown in Figure 2B demonstrating negative asymmetry values.

claim: There is a significant difference between the asymmetry profiles of the closed (M = –0.06, SD = 0.33) and open (M = –1.68, SD = 0.89) conformations (p<0.001).
source: There is a significant difference between the asymmetry profiles of the closed (M = –0.06, SD = 0.33) and open (M = –1.68, SD = 0.89) conformations (p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical comparison of DCIasym distributions between conformations shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The hACE2 binding site is dominated by the dynamics of the CAPs in closed chains when the S protein is in its pre-fusion conformation with one chain open.
source: This indicates an allosteric control where the hACE2 binding site is dominated by the dynamics of the CAPs in closed chains (Figure 2B, yellow bars).
evidence: Interpretation of DCIasym results showing allosteric control mechanism.

claim: Residues responsible for extremely low asymmetry values (<–4) lie overwhelmingly in the region 476–486.
source: Interestingly, residues responsible for extremely low asymmetry values (<–4) lie overwhelmingly in the region 476–486.
evidence: Analysis of DCIasym data identifying specific residue region.

claim: Residues in region 476-486 were suggested to stabilize S protein dynamics and prime it for host Furin proteolysis.
source: These same residues were suggested to stabilize S protein dynamics and prime it for host Furin proteolysis (Raghuvamsi et al., 2021).
evidence: Reference to prior study about functional role of these residues.

claim: The DCIasym of the CAPs residue positions with respect to the hACE2 interface in the closed configuration yields a largely symmetric distribution about 0.
source: Moreover, as a control, we performed the same analysis on the S protein with the RBDs of all chains in the closed configuration. In this case, we observed that the DCIasym of the CAPs residue positions with respect to the hACE2 interface in the other chains yields a largely symmetric distribution about 0 (Figure 2B, green bars).
evidence: Control experiment results shown in Figure 2B demonstrating symmetric distribution.

claim: The COVID-19 S protein shows high correlation (r = 0.94) between the occurrence of mutations and site flexibility.
source: We found that the COVID-19 S protein shows the expected high correlation between the occurrence of mutations and site flexibility (Figure 3) when we compare %DFI (DFI ranked by percentile) to the average number of variants per position found within a given %DFI bin.
evidence: Correlation analysis shown in Figure 3 with caption stating r = 0.94.

claim: More rigid residues tend to have fewer variants.
source: More rigid residues tend to have fewer variants (r = 0.94).
evidence: Figure 3 caption and analysis showing inverse relationship between rigidity and variant count.

claim: Rigid residues are critical for functional dynamics and more likely to impact function if mutated.
source: Previous studies have indicated that rigid residues are critical for functional dynamics, thus more likely to impact function if mutated and, generally, can lead to a loss of function and thus more conserved (Kim et al., 2015; Butler et al., 2018; Modi et al., 2021b; Modi et al., 2021a; Kazan et al., 2022; Ose et al., 2022a; Stevens et al., 2022; Kumar et al., 2015).
evidence: Summary of findings from multiple cited studies.

claim: VOC emergence is punctuated by an episodic period of rapid evolution, with a substitution rate of up to fourfold greater than the background substitution rate.
source: Indeed, by fitting various molecular clock models to genome sequence data, VOC emergence is punctuated by an episodic period of rapid evolution, with a substitution rate of up to fourfold greater than the background substitution rate (Kumar et al., 2021; Tay et al., 2022).
evidence: Reference to molecular clock modeling studies.

claim: Delta mutation sites (M = –0.98, SD = 0.80) have less allosteric control over the hACE2 binding sites than Omicron mutation sites (M = –1.74, SD = 1.00) (p<0.001).
source: Delta displays a second peak closer to zero, suggesting that Delta mutation sites (M = –0.98, SD = 0.80) have less allosteric control over the hACE2 binding sites than Omicron mutation sites (M = –1.74, SD = 1.00) (p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical comparison of DCIasym values between Delta and Omicron shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Both Delta and Omicron mutation sites have far more control over hACE2 binding sites than expected based on a random control group (M = 0.03, SD = 0.85) (p<0.001).
source: However, both sets of sites have far more control over hACE2 binding sites than expected, based on a random control group (M = 0.03, SD = 0.85) (p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical comparison with random control shown in Figure 4A.

claim: EpiScore has previously been used successfully to capture overarching trends in GB1 deep mutational scan data as well as specific instances of the development of antibiotic resistance in various enzymatic systems.
source: EpiScore has previously been used successfully to capture overarching trends in GB1 deep mutational scan data as well as specific instances of the development of antibiotic resistance in various enzymatic systems (Campitelli and Ozkan, 2020).
evidence: Reference to prior validation of the EpiScore method.

claim: EpiScore results and experimentally determined epistasis both captured highly epistatic behavior among residues 493, 496, 498, 501, and 505.
source: Our EpiScore results and the experimentally determined epistasis both captured highly epistatic behavior among residues 493, 496, 498, 501, and 505, as well as a lack of epistatic behavior for residues 339, 371, 373, and 375
evidence: Comparison between computational EpiScore and experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: EpiScore showed a lack of epistatic behavior for residues 339, 371, 373, and 375.
source: Our EpiScore results and the experimentally determined epistasis both captured highly epistatic behavior among residues 493, 496, 498, 501, and 505, as well as a lack of epistatic behavior for residues 339, 371, 373, and 375
evidence: Comparison between computational EpiScore and experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: EpiScore generally showed higher epistasis values than experiment for residues 417, 440, 446, 477, 478, and 484.
source: however, EpiScore generally showed higher epistasis values than experiment for residues 417, 440, 446, 477, 478, and 484.
evidence: Comparison between computational and experimental results showing discrepancies.

claim: Omicron shows a high proportion of additive mutations compared to the Delta variant, with a peak centered on 1.
source: To contrast these variants, Omicron (Figure 6, cyan) shows a high proportion of additive mutations compared to the Delta variant (Figure 6, magenta), with a peak centered on 1.
evidence: EpiScore distribution analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The comparatively more pathogenic Delta variant exhibited many non-additive mutations with EpiScores below one.
source: The comparatively more pathogenic Delta variant exhibited many non-additive mutations with EpiScores below one.
evidence: EpiScore distribution analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Four out of seven low EP Delta mutation sites used in this analysis often resulted in EpiScores below 1.
source: Four out of seven low EP Delta mutation sites used in this analysis often resulted in EpiScores below 1.
evidence: Analysis of EpiScore data for Delta mutation sites.

claim: Delta NTD mutations are found on or near the N3 loop and are implicated in antibody escape in recent studies.
source: Each of those is found in the N-terminal domain (NTD) on or near the N3 loop and is implicated in antibody escape in recent studies (Chi et al., 2020; Weisblum et al., 2020; Harvey et al., 2021; Klinakis et al., 2021; Cantoni et al., 2022).
evidence: Reference to multiple studies identifying functional role of NTD mutations.

claim: The low EpiScores of NTD mutations suggest that they dampen the control of Wuhan variant CAPs over the hACE2 binding sites in addition to their effects on antibody binding.
source: The low EpiScores of NTD mutations suggest that they dampen the control of Wuhan variant CAPs over the hACE2 binding sites in addition to their effects on antibody binding.
evidence: Interpretation of EpiScore results for NTD mutations.

claim: The mutations leading to the development of the Omicron strain were additive with respect to Wuhan variant CAPs, possibly leading to a lower pathogenicity and higher effective immune escape.
source: In contrast, the mutations leading to the development of the Omicron strain were additive with respect to Wuhan variant CAPs, possibly leading to a lower pathogenicity and higher effective immune escape, resulting in an overall higher transmission rate.
evidence: Interpretation of EpiScore results connecting additivity to phenotypic outcomes.

claim: Despite reduced binding affinity with hACE2, Omicron showed increased occupancy of the open state compared to the closed state.
source: Another possible explanation for the higher transmission rate of Omicron comes from a different normal mode analysis study, which found that despite reduced binding affinity with hACE2, Omicron showed increased occupancy of the open state compared to the closed state, which would increase chances of interaction with hACE2 (Teruel et al., 2021b).
evidence: Reference to another study's findings about Omicron conformational dynamics.

claim: NTD mutation sites result in markedly lower EpiScores compared to elsewhere (p<0.001).
source: NTD mutation sites result in markedly lower EpiScores compared to elsewhere (p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical comparison shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Three CAPs (346R, 486F, and 498Q) are responsible for the tail of EpiScore values upward of 2.0, indicating highly epistatic behavior.
source: One of the more notable features of generated EpiScore distributions is the presence of a tail of values upward of 2.0, indicating highly epistatic behavior. Interestingly, these tails are largely due to three different CAPs: 346R, 486F, and 498Q.
evidence: Analysis of EpiScore distribution identifying specific residues.

claim: Residues 346R and 486F are known antibody binding sites.
source: Those residues are nearby one another within the protein structure and have been reported to play a role in antibody binding, either being known antibody binding sites (346R and 486F) or having received very high antibody accessibility scores (498Q) (Harvey et al., 2021; Raghuvamsi et al., 2021).
evidence: Reference to studies identifying antibody binding sites.

claim: Residue 498Q has received very high antibody accessibility scores.
source: Those residues are nearby one another within the protein structure and have been reported to play a role in antibody binding, either being known antibody binding sites (346R and 486F) or having received very high antibody accessibility scores (498Q) (Harvey et al., 2021; Raghuvamsi et al., 2021).
evidence: Reference to studies assessing antibody accessibility.

claim: The epistatic interactions between CAPs 346R, 486F, 498Q and the mutations of the VOCs within the S protein are crucial for maintaining binding affinity of hACE2 whilst evading immunity.
source: These observed high EpiScore values also support other studies indicating the epistatic interactions between these CAPs and the mutations of the VOCs within the S protein are crucial for maintaining binding affinity of hACE2 whilst evading immunity (Hong et al., 2022; Starr et al., 2022b).
evidence: EpiScore results supporting findings from other studies.

claim: Site 486F is a binding site for both hACE2 and antibodies.
source: Inspection of EpiScores of Delta and Omicron potentially adaptive mutation sites with only CAP site 486F (a binding site for both hACE2 and antibodies) (Huang et al., 2020; Ali et al., 2021; Harvey et al., 2021; Raghuvamsi et al., 2021) shows highly epistatic interactions at other hACE2 binding sites (Figure 6).
evidence: Reference to multiple studies identifying dual binding function.

claim: Within XBB 1.5, there is a mutation of S to P at site 486, a rare double nucleotide mutation.
source: However, within a recent and rapidly spreading subvariant of Omicron, XBB 1.5, we see a mutation of S to P, a rare double nucleotide mutation, at site 486 (preceding Omicron variants included mutation F486S from the original CAP).
evidence: Description of specific mutation in XBB 1.5 variant.

claim: XBB 1.5 has unprecedented immune escape capabilities, resisting neutralizing antibodies almost entirely.
source: This new variant has unprecedented immune escape capabilities, resisting neutralizing antibodies almost entirely (Qu et al., 2023).
evidence: Reference to study characterizing XBB 1.5 immune escape.

claim: EpiScores of other XBB 1.5-specific mutation sites with 486P are almost entirely greater than 1, showing an even higher degree of epistasis with the binding sites of RBD.
source: EpiScores of other XBB 1.5-specific mutation sites with 486P are almost entirely greater than 1, showing an even higher degree of epistasis with the binding sites of RBD (Figure 7).
evidence: EpiScore analysis results shown in Figure 7.

claim: CAP and hACE2 and antibody binding site 486 displays epistasis with almost all XBB 1.5 variant sites at almost every hACE2 binding site (M = 1.40, SD = 0.46) and presents a significantly different profile from other variant sites (p<0.01).
source: CAP and hACE2 and antibody binding site 486 displays epistasis with almost all XBB 1.5 variant sites at almost every hACE2 binding site (M = 1.40, SD = 0.46) and presents a significantly different profile from other variant sites (p<0.01).
evidence: Statistical analysis of EpiScore data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The S486P mutation is responsible for modifying hACE2 binding via epistatic cooperation with other co-occurring mutations.
source: These results present a threefold importance for the S486P mutation: not only does this residue alter antibody (i.e., immune escape) and hACE2 binding by directly modifying a binding site, but it may also be responsible for modifying hACE2 binding via epistatic cooperation with other co-occurring mutations.
evidence: Interpretation of EpiScore results for S486P mutation.

claim: Characteristic mutations on the RBD in the Omicron variant are shown to increase the overall binding affinity of the virus to the ACE2 receptor.
source: Within the Omicron variant, for example, characteristic mutations on the RBD are shown to increase the overall binding affinity of the virus to the ACE2 receptor, which is suspected to allow it to spread more easily (Kim et al., 2021).
evidence: Reference to study showing increased binding affinity.

claim: The trend of total %DFI with the log of Kd values overlaps with the one seen with the experiments (r = 0.97).
source: The trend of total %DFI with the log of Kd values overlaps with the one seen with the experiments (r = 0.97).
evidence: Correlation analysis shown in Figure 8B comparing computational and experimental results.

claim: The Omicron XBB variant exhibits heightened flexibility in hACE2 and antibody binding residues, reducing infectivity and enhancing immune evasion.
source: The Omicron XBB variant exhibits heightened flexibility in hACE2 and antibody binding residues, reducing infectivity and enhancing immune evasion.
evidence: Analysis of DFI profiles from MD simulations shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The Omicron XBB 1.5 variant induces distinct dynamics in hACE2 and antibody binding regions, rendering the RBD-ACE2 interface more rigid while increasing flexibility in antibody binding residues.
source: Conversely, the Omicron XBB 1.5 variant induces distinct dynamics in these regions, rendering the RBD-ACE2 interface more rigid while increasing flexibility in antibody binding residues.
evidence: Analysis of DFI profiles from MD simulations shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Omicron XBB 1.5 retains its antibody escape capabilities while regaining ACE2 binding affinity comparable to previous Omicron variants, in accordance with experimental findings.
source: These effects indicate that Omicron XBB 1.5 retains its antibody escape capabilities while regaining ACE2 binding affinity comparable to previous Omicron variants, in accordance with experimental findings (Yue et al., 2023).
evidence: Interpretation of DFI results supported by experimental reference.

claim: Mutations in the RBD and antibody binding residues can have complex effects on the dynamics of the protein and on the virus's ability to infect and evade the host immune system through an alteration of binding site dynamics.
source: These findings suggest that mutations in the RBD and antibody binding residues can have complex effects on the dynamics of the protein and, ultimately, on the virus's ability to infect and evade the host immune system through an alteration of binding site dynamics.
evidence: General conclusion drawn from DFI analysis results.

claim: The effects of a mutation will heavily depend on the genetic background in which they are mutated.
source: However, we do note that the effect of mutations will heavily depend on the genetic background in which they are mutated. The effects of a mutation on a Delta variant protein may differ entirely from the effects of a mutation on an Omicron variant protein (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Statement about context-dependence of mutations supported by supplementary figure.

claim: The Omicron variant has a lower binding affinity with hACE2 than previous variants.
source: It has also been shown that the Omicron variant has a lower binding affinity with hACE2 than previous variants (Wu et al., 2022), which may contribute to its low pathogenicity.
evidence: Reference to experimental study measuring binding affinity.

claim: The RBD exhibits both 'closed' and 'open' conformational states.
source: The RBD exhibits both 'closed' and 'open' conformational states. In the closed state, the RBD is shielded from receptor binding. In the open state, the RBD is accessible for hACE2 binding (Kirchdoerfer et al., 2016; Gur et al., 2020; Henderson et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2020).
evidence: Description of RBD conformational states supported by multiple citations.

claim: Some mutations may affect the transition between closed and open RBD states.
source: While some mutations may affect the transition between these states (Henderson et al., 2020; Yurkovetskiy et al., 2020; Gobeil et al., 2021a; Sztain et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021; Shoemark et al., 2022), other mutations may allosterically regulate RBD openings through Furin cleavage site (residue ID range: 681–695) interactions to regulate hACE2 binding (Deng et al., 2021; Gobeil et al., 2021b; Khan et al., 2021; Laiton-Donato et al., 2021).
evidence: Summary of findings from multiple studies about mutation effects.

claim: Other mutations may allosterically regulate RBD openings through Furin cleavage site interactions to regulate hACE2 binding.
source: While some mutations may affect the transition between these states (Henderson et al., 2020; Yurkovetskiy et al., 2020; Gobeil et al., 2021a; Sztain et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021; Shoemark et al., 2022), other mutations may allosterically regulate RBD openings through Furin cleavage site (residue ID range: 681–695) interactions to regulate hACE2 binding (Deng et al., 2021; Gobeil et al., 2021b; Khan et al., 2021; Laiton-Donato et al., 2021).
evidence: Summary of findings from multiple studies about allosteric regulation.

claim: VOCs result in a substantial difference in protein function compared to their individual mutation effects.
source: While many studies have explored the impacts of individual mutations, VOCs result in a substantial difference in protein function compared to their individual effects (Moulana et al., 2022; Starr et al., 2022c; Moulana et al., 2023; Witte et al., 2023).
evidence: Reference to studies demonstrating non-additive effects in VOCs.

claim: F486 and Q498 have already been identified through perturbation response scanning as potential allosteric sites.
source: However, our study will focus mainly on the role of CAPs, of which F486 and Q498 have already been identified through perturbation response scanning (PRS) as potential allosteric sites (Verkhivker, 2022).
evidence: Reference to prior study identifying allosteric sites.

claim: Binding affinity with hACE2 can be enhanced directly through stronger receptor interactions or mediated through changes in RBD opening.
source: Binding affinity with hACE2 can be enhanced directly through stronger receptor interactions or mediated through changes in RBD opening (Teruel et al., 2021b; Zhang et al., 2021; Díaz-Salinas et al., 2022).
evidence: Summary of mechanisms from cited studies.

claim: Fine-tuning S protein interactions with hACE2 significantly affects viral reproduction.
source: Evidence indicates that fine-tuning S protein interactions with hACE2 significantly affects viral reproduction (Rehman et al., 2020; Saputri et al., 2020; Rochman et al., 2021).
evidence: Reference to studies showing relationship between binding and reproduction.

claim: Previous evolutionary studies show a complex network of interactions among mutated residues.
source: Previous evolutionary studies show a complex network of interactions among mutated residues (Changeux and Edelstein, 2005; Doshi et al., 2016; O'Rourke et al., 2016; Mishra and Jernigan, 2018).
evidence: Reference to multiple studies demonstrating interaction networks.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 has continuously mutated since its early detection.
source: This is because SARS-CoV-2 has continuously mutated since its early detection (Kistler et al., 2022), causing the emergence of CDC-designated 'variants of concern' (VOCs) that may be driven by an accelerated substitution rate (Tay et al., 2022).
evidence: Reference to studies documenting continuous mutation.

claim: The S glycoprotein of SARS-CoV-2 binds to the human ACE2 receptor through its receptor-binding domain for successful infection of a human host.
source: For successful infection of a human host, the S glycoprotein of SARS-CoV-2 binds to the human ACE2 (hACE2) receptor through its receptor-binding domain (RBD).
evidence: Description of fundamental mechanism of viral infection.

claim: The S protein has been one of the most studied and targeted proteins in SARS-CoV-2 research.
source: The S protein is directly related to the human immune response to COVID-19 and, as such, has been one of the most studied and targeted proteins in SARS-CoV-2 research (Shang et al., 2020; Harvey et al., 2021; Jackson et al., 2022; Carabelli et al., 2023; Markov et al., 2023).
evidence: Statement about research focus supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mutations modulate conformational dynamics, leading to changes in biophysical properties such as stability, flexibility, and allosteric dynamic coupling.
source: In particular, we focused on how mutations modulate protein dynamics as we and others have previously found that rather than changing a protein's structure solely, mutations modulate conformational dynamics, leading to changes in biophysical properties such as stability, flexibility, and allosteric dynamic coupling, any of which may affect protein binding (Swint-Kruse et al., 1998; Keskin et al., 2000; Bhabha et al., 2013; Nussinov and Tsai, 2013; Campbell et al., 2016; Ma and Nussinov, 2016; Saavedra et al., 2018; Kuzmanic et al., 2020).
evidence: Summary of findings from multiple studies about mutation effects on dynamics.

claim: CAPs are substitutions in SARS-CoV-2 that are rarely observed in other closely related sequences, which implies a degree of functional importance and makes them candidates for adaptation.
source: CAPs are substitutions in SARS-CoV-2 that are rarely observed in other closely related sequences (Figure 1A), which implies a degree of functional importance and makes them candidates for adaptation (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: Definition of CAPs with reference to method and figure.

claim: CAPs may be partially responsible for the functional change allowing the infection of human hosts.
source: Therefore, we suspect that these CAPs may be partially responsible for the functional change allowing the infection of human hosts.
evidence: Hypothesis based on CAP identification and their properties.

claim: CAPs can be compensatory; multiple CAPs may dynamically compensate for one another, changing the dynamic landscape and allowing for different mutations.
source: In addition, our earlier work has shown that CAPS can also be compensatory; multiple CAPs may dynamically compensate for one another, changing the dynamic landscape and allowing for different mutations (Ose et al., 2022b).
evidence: Reference to prior work on compensatory mutations.

claim: Allosteric sites exert control over the dynamics of the binding sites, and mutations of these allosteric sites modulate function.
source: We find a mechanistic pattern in the S protein evolution that is common amongst previously studied systems, where allosteric sites exert control over the dynamics of the binding sites, and mutations of these allosteric sites modulate function.
evidence: General conclusion from dynamics analysis.

claim: Many allosteric sites regulating function of the S protein may have been subjected to adaptive evolution as observed in mutations in VOCs.
source: Coupling our analysis with evolutionary theory showed that many of these allosteric sites regulating function of the S protein may have been subjected to adaptive evolution as observed in mutations in VOCs.
evidence: Integration of dynamics and evolutionary analysis results.

claim: The Omicron-defining sites have greater control over the binding sites than the Delta variant and are dynamically additive with the functional advantage of CAPs.
source: Our dynamics analysis also provides a mechanistic insight where the Omicron-defining sites have greater control over the binding sites than the Delta variant and are dynamically additive with the functional advantage of CAPs, thus, the greatest infectivity may not be a coincidence.
evidence: Interpretation of DCIasym and EpiScore results.

claim: The interactions between CAP sites and VOC-defining mutations show fingerprints of non-additive dynamics within the Delta variant.
source: Specifically, we find that the interactions between CAP sites and VOC-defining mutations show fingerprints of non-additive dynamics within the Delta variant.
evidence: Summary of EpiScore analysis for Delta variant.

claim: Mutations leading to the Omicron variant are largely additive, driving critical dynamical behavior closer to the patterns observed within the wild-type.
source: In contrast, mutations leading to the Omicron variant are largely additive, driving critical dynamical behavior closer to the patterns observed within the wild-type.
evidence: Summary of EpiScore analysis for Omicron variant.

claim: Long-ranged interactions between different sites within a given protein are critically important for protein function.
source: Long-ranged interactions between different sites within a given protein are critically important for protein function (Peters and Lively, 1999; Bershtein et al., 2006; Collins et al., 2006; Ekeberg et al., 2013; Levy et al., 2017; Harrigan et al., 2018; Otten et al., 2018; Rojas Echenique et al., 2019; Shimagaki and Weigt, 2019; de la Paz et al., 2020; Rizzato et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020; Bisardi et al., 2022) and for the CoV-2 S protein in particular (Zeng et al., 2020; Castiglione et al., 2021; Dong et al., 2021; Garvin et al., 2021; Nielsen et al., 2022; Ramarao-Milne et al., 2022; Rochman et al., 2022; Rodriguez-Rivas et al., 2022).
evidence: Summary of findings from extensive literature on long-range interactions.

claim: CAP sites are of continued importance to protein function and should be given special attention when considering the impact of future mutations.
source: In addition to supporting previous dynamic research on the S protein, this analysis provides the insight that CAP sites are of continued importance to protein function and should be given special attention when considering the impact of future mutations.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comprehensive analysis of CAPs across variants.

claim: Omicron subvariants are of growing concern due in large part to further increased immune evasion.
source: As variants continue to evolve, Omicron subvariants are of growing concern due in large part to further increased immune evasion (Callaway, 2022; Wang et al., 2022a; Wang et al., 2022b), and we observe that the new mutations observed in antibody binding sites yield more epistatic interaction with the CAPs.
evidence: Reference to studies documenting immune evasion concerns.

claim: New mutations observed in antibody binding sites yield more epistatic interaction with the CAPs.
source: As variants continue to evolve, Omicron subvariants are of growing concern due in large part to further increased immune evasion (Callaway, 2022; Wang et al., 2022a; Wang et al., 2022b), and we observe that the new mutations observed in antibody binding sites yield more epistatic interaction with the CAPs.
evidence: EpiScore analysis of Omicron subvariants.

claim: EpiScores using sites of either variant (Delta: M = 0.70, SD = 0.50, Omicron M = 0.86, SD = 0.46) are significantly different (p<0.001) from a set of EpiScores using random sites (M = 0.84, SD = 0.41).
source: EpiScores using sites of either variant (Delta: M = 0.70, SD = 0.50, Omicron M = 0.86, SD = 0.46) are significantly different (p<0.001) from a set of EpiScores using random sites (M = 0.84, SD = 0.41), but the distribution for Delta variants differs much more from the other two.
evidence: Statistical comparison shown in Figure 6.

claim: The distribution for Delta variants differs much more from random and Omicron than Omicron differs from random.
source: EpiScores using sites of either variant (Delta: M = 0.70, SD = 0.50, Omicron M = 0.86, SD = 0.46) are significantly different (p<0.001) from a set of EpiScores using random sites (M = 0.84, SD = 0.41), but the distribution for Delta variants differs much more from the other two.
evidence: Statistical comparison shown in Figure 6.

claim: The asymmetry in the coupling of CAPs with the exposed binding site interface in pre-fusion configuration results from one of the RBDs opening up.
source: This verifies that the asymmetry in the coupling of CAPs with the exposed binding site interface in pre-fusion configuration results from one of the RBDs opening up and further suggests the allosteric role played by CAPs in locking the S protein in the RBD open state.
evidence: Interpretation of control experiment comparing open and closed conformations.

claim: CAPs play an allosteric role in locking the S protein in the RBD open state.
source: This verifies that the asymmetry in the coupling of CAPs with the exposed binding site interface in pre-fusion configuration results from one of the RBDs opening up and further suggests the allosteric role played by CAPs in locking the S protein in the RBD open state.
evidence: Interpretation of DCIasym results for open vs closed conformations.

claim: Residue positions with CAP substitutions hold the potential for mutations in the spike sequence which can alter the opening and closing dynamics of the RBD.
source: Similarly, it is possible that mutations to such residue positions within the S protein can be used to regulate the dynamics of the hACE2 bindings sites of the open RBD state. We, therefore, propose that the residue positions with CAP substitutions hold the potential for mutations in the spike sequence which can alter the opening and closing dynamics of the RBD.
evidence: Hypothesis based on DCIasym analysis and comparison with LacI system.

claim: Mutations at CAP residue positions alter the infection rate.
source: This hypothesis is further supported by many mutations already observed at these residue positions which alter the infection rate (Brister et al., 2015).
evidence: Reference to database showing mutations at CAP sites affecting infection.

claim: Cross-chain communication within the main protease of SARS COV-2 is enhanced compared to SARS COV-1.
source: Recent work from our group has shown an enhancement in cross-chain communication within the main protease of SARS COV-2 compared to SARS COV-1 (Campitelli et al., 2022).
evidence: Reference to prior work on cross-chain communication.

claim: Allosteric inter-chain communication is important to S protein function.
source: Furthermore, previous studies have shown that allosteric inter-chain communication is important to S protein function (Zhou et al., 2020; Spinello et al., 2021; Tan et al., 2022; Xue et al., 2022).
evidence: Reference to multiple studies on inter-chain communication.

claim: The open-state RBD is critical for the viral infection of host cells.
source: As this open-state RBD is critical for the viral infection of host cells (Kirchdoerfer et al., 2016), our results suggest that this type of closed-to-open cross-chain interaction is important for viral proliferation.
evidence: Reference to study on RBD function combined with DCIasym results.

claim: Allosteric mutations that alter DNA binding affinity in LacI exhibited unique asymmetry profiles with the DNA binding sites and regulated the dynamics of these binding sites.
source: Our prior studies on DCIasym show a similar trend in lactose inhibitor (LacI), a protein with a functional role in gene expression through binding DNA. The allosteric mutations (i.e., mutations on the sites that are far from the DNA binding sites) that alter DNA binding affinity not only exhibited unique asymmetry profiles with the DNA binding sites of LacI, but also regulated the dynamics of these binding sites (Campitelli et al., 2021).
evidence: Reference to prior work on LacI showing similar patterns.

claim: The rate of evolution per positional site exhibits a positive correlation with positional flexibility.
source: Our previous work has indicated that the rate of evolution per positional site exhibits a positive correlation with positional flexibility; generally, positions that exhibit higher flexibility are also sites that experience a higher number of amino acid substitutions (Liu and Bahar, 2012; Maguid et al., 2008; Maguid et al., 2006; Mikulska-Ruminska et al., 2019; Nevin Gerek et al., 2013).
evidence: Reference to multiple studies showing correlation between flexibility and evolution.

claim: Certain highly observed mutations make the open state more rigid and the closed state more flexible.
source: For example, Teruel et al., 2021a used their Elastic Network Contact Model to find how certain highly observed mutations make the open state more rigid and the closed state more flexible.
evidence: Reference to specific study on mutation effects on conformational states.

claim: Deleterious mutations on rigid positions should be eliminated and therefore not observed according to neutral theory of molecular evolution.
source: This analysis also agrees with these previous studies and highlights the power of negative selection, in line with the neutral theory of molecular evolution, stating that deleterious mutations (i.e., those on the rigid positions) should be eliminated and therefore not observed (Kimura, 1983).
evidence: Reference to neutral theory and interpretation of flexibility-mutation correlation.

claim: Mutational data was calculated across approximately 24,000 SARS-CoV-2 S protein sequences from the NCBI Datasets Project.
source: Mutational data was calculated across approximately 24,000 SARS-CoV-2 S protein sequences from the NCBI Datasets Project (Brister et al., 2015).
evidence: Description of data source in Figure 3 caption.

claim: Residue flexibility was computed using PDB id 6vsb from the Protein DataBank.
source: Residue flexibility, as reported here via %DFI, was computed using PDB id 6vsb from the Protein DataBank (Berman et al., 2000).
evidence: Description of structure source in Figure 3 caption.

claim: The difference in virulence and infection rates between Omicron and Delta might be due to specific CAPs within each variant and their differences in allosterically controlling the dynamics of open RBD binding sites.
source: We surmise that the difference in virulence and infection rates between Omicron and Delta (Earnest et al., 2022; Bager et al., 2021; Sheikh et al., 2021; Twohig et al., 2022; Houhamdi et al., 2022; Menni et al., 2022) might be due to these specific CAPs within each variant and their differences in allosterically controlling the dynamics of open RBD binding sites as also observed in the DCIasym analysis of the Wuhan variant in Figure 2.
evidence: Hypothesis connecting DCIasym results to phenotypic differences, supported by citations.

claim: The asymmetry is much more pronounced in observed mutations of Omicron variants compared to Delta variants.
source: Regarding this, we see that the asymmetry is much more pronounced in observed mutations of Omicron variants, suggesting that these new mutations have a stronger power in controlling the dynamics of open-chain hACE2 binding interface compared to those observed in Delta variants.
evidence: Comparison of DCIasym distributions shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Omicron mutations have a stronger power in controlling the dynamics of open-chain hACE2 binding interface compared to Delta mutations.
source: Regarding this, we see that the asymmetry is much more pronounced in observed mutations of Omicron variants, suggesting that these new mutations have a stronger power in controlling the dynamics of open-chain hACE2 binding interface compared to those observed in Delta variants.
evidence: Interpretation of DCIasym comparison between variants.

claim: Studies of evolutionary pathways of mutations have suggested that a majority of the mutations have a second or a higher order epistasis among them.
source: In fact, studies of evolutionary pathways of mutations have suggested that a majority of the mutations have a second or a higher order epistasis among them (Bershtein et al., 2006).
evidence: Reference to study on epistasis in evolutionary pathways.

claim: Nature exploits higher order complex relationships between mutations to evolve their function.
source: Nature exploits this higher order complex relationship between the mutations to evolve their function.
evidence: General statement about evolutionary mechanisms.

claim: An EpiScore of 1 indicates perfect coupling additivity.
source: An EpiScore of 1 indicates perfect coupling additivity, and deviations from this value represent non-additive behavior between position pairs and functionally important sites.
evidence: Definition of EpiScore metric interpretation.

claim: Non-compensatory mutations show higher deviation in their EpiScore distribution compared to compensatory mutations.
source: Prior EpiScore work has shown a difference in EpiScore between the sites of compensatory and non-compensatory mutations, where both yield distributions with peaks around 1, but non-compensatory mutations show higher deviation in their EpiScore distribution (Ose et al., 2022b).
evidence: Reference to prior work characterizing EpiScore distributions.

claim: Many studies have confirmed epistasis between residues within the S protein.
source: Many studies have confirmed epistasis between residues within the S protein (Moulana et al., 2022; Starr et al., 2022a; Moulana et al., 2023; Witte et al., 2023).
evidence: Reference to multiple studies confirming epistasis.

claim: Epistatic residues can have various effects on hACE2 or antibody binding.
source: These epistatic residues can have various effects on hACE2 or antibody binding.
evidence: General statement about functional consequences of epistasis.

claim: Interactions between Omicron and Delta variants show similar behavior to hospitalization rates.
source: These interactions may also drive observed behavior similar between the reference and Omicron strains yet differ in the delta strain, such as the severity of infection as evidenced by hospitalization rates (Houhamdi et al., 2022; Menni et al., 2022).
evidence: Connection between EpiScore results and clinical outcomes, supported by citations.

claim: What the Delta variant gained in transmission rate also came with being more harmfully pathogenic due in part to negatively epistatic interactions.
source: It is possible that what the Delta variant gained in transmission rate also came with being more harmfully pathogenic due in part to negatively epistatic interactions.
evidence: Hypothesis connecting EpiScore results to pathogenicity.

claim: The S486P mutation alters antibody and hACE2 binding by directly modifying a binding site.
source: These results present a threefold importance for the S486P mutation: not only does this residue alter antibody (i.e., immune escape) and hACE2 binding by directly modifying a binding site, but it may also be responsible for modifying hACE2 binding via epistatic cooperation with other co-occurring mutations.
evidence: Interpretation of EpiScore results for S486P mutation.

claim: The Furin cleavage site is located at residues 676-689.
source: We observe that a majority of the CAP positions reside at the receptor-binding domain (RBD) and the Furin cleavage site (676-689; Wrobel et al., 2020) shown as transparent light gray spheres.
evidence: Specific residue range provided with citation in Figure 1C caption.

claim: Host cell protease TMPRSS2 facilitates viral attachment to the surface of target cells upon binding either to sites Arg815/Ser816, or Arg685/Ser686 which overlap with the Furin cleavage site 676–689.
source: Another host cell protease, TMPRSS2, facilitates viral attachment to the surface of target cells upon binding either to sites Arg815/Ser816, or Arg685/Ser686 which overlap with the Furin cleavage site 676–689, further emphasizing the importance of this area (; Fraser et al., 2022).
evidence: Description of TMPRSS2 binding sites with citation.

claim: Similar cleavage sites have been found in related coronaviruses, including HKU1 and MERS-CoV, which infects humans.
source: Similar cleavage sites have been found in related coronaviruses, including HKU1 and Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV), which infects humans (Chan et al., 2008: 1; Millet and Whittaker, 2014; Millet and Whittaker, 2015)
evidence: Reference to studies identifying cleavage sites in related viruses.

claim: The acquisition of similar cleavage sites is associated with increased pathogenicity in other viruses such as the influenza virus.
source: and the acquisition of similar cleavage sites is associated with increased pathogenicity in other viruses such as the influenza virus (Steinhauer, 1999).
evidence: Reference to study on cleavage sites and pathogenicity in influenza.

claim: CAPs do not display an overwhelming tendency to occur at well-known critical sites within human proteins studied with similar methods.
source: Interestingly, however, CAPs do not display such an overwhelming tendency to occur at well-known critical sites within human proteins studied with similar methods (Ose et al., 2022b), yet mutations at those sites are associated with disease, indicating their critical role in inducing functional change.
evidence: Comparison with prior work on human proteins.

claim: Mutations at CAP sites in human proteins are associated with disease, indicating their critical role in inducing functional change.
source: Interestingly, however, CAPs do not display such an overwhelming tendency to occur at well-known critical sites within human proteins studied with similar methods (Ose et al., 2022b), yet mutations at those sites are associated with disease, indicating their critical role in inducing functional change.
evidence: Reference to prior work on disease-associated mutations.

claim: EP scores of amino acid variants of the S protein were obtained using a maximum likelihood phylogeny built from 19 orthologous coronavirus sequences.
source: EP scores of the amino acid variants of the S protein were obtained using a maximum likelihood phylogeny (Kumar et al., 2018) built from 19 orthologous coronavirus sequences.
evidence: Description of phylogenetic method used.

claim: Sequences were selected by examining available non-human sequences with a sequence identity of 70% or above to the human SARS CoV-2's S protein sequence.
source: Sequences were selected by examining available non-human sequences with a sequence identity of 70% or above to the human SARS CoV-2's S protein sequence.
evidence: Description of sequence selection criteria.

claim: The 70% sequence identity cutoff allows for divergence over evolutionary history such that each amino acid position had ample time to experience purifying selection, whilst limiting ourselves to closely related coronaviruses.
source: This cutoff allows for divergence over evolutionary history such that each amino acid position had ample time to experience purifying selection, whilst limiting ourselves to closely related coronaviruses.
evidence: Justification for sequence selection criteria.

claim: The likelihood of finding a particular amino acid in the sequence is determined using a Bayesian framework, with calculations carried out by MEGA X software.
source: The likelihood of finding a particular amino acid in the sequence is then determined using a Bayesian framework, with calculations carried out by MEGA X software (Kumar et al., 2018).
evidence: Description of computational method with software citation.

claim: Amino acid residues receiving low EP scores (<0.05) at a position are less likely to be found in a given position within the sequence because they are non-neutral.
source: Amino acid residues receiving low EP scores (<0.05) at a position are less likely to be found in a given position within the sequence because they are non-neutral.
evidence: Interpretation of EP scores based on neutral theory.

claim: Positions with low EP amino acids are far less common than those containing mutations with high EP.
source: Generally, positions with low EP amino acids are far less common than those containing mutations with high EP, a trend also realized in the CoV-2 S protein (Figure 1B).
evidence: Observation from EP distribution shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Fixation of a low EP amino acid at a position suggests an underlying mechanism for natural selection to operate.
source: While amino acids with low EP should be harmful or deleterious to viral fitness due to functional disruption or change, fixation of a low EP amino acid at a position suggests an underlying mechanism for natural selection to operate.
evidence: Interpretation based on evolutionary theory.

claim: Fixed, low EP mutations are called CAPs as they are predicted to alter protein function, and adaptive pressures may drive their prevalence.
source: These fixed, low EP mutations are called CAPs as they are predicted to alter protein function, and adaptive pressures may drive their prevalence (Kumar and Patel, 2018).
evidence: Definition of CAPs with citation.

claim: The remaining 11 CAPs are undiscovered candidate sites for adaptation.
source: Within these studies, sites 478, 486, 498, and 681 have been implicated in SARS-CoV-2 evolution, leaving the remaining 11 CAPs as undiscovered candidate sites for adaptation.
evidence: Calculation based on total CAPs minus previously identified sites.

claim: Before ACE2 binding, one chain of the homotrimer comprising the S protein must open to expose the RBD.
source: Before ACE2 binding, one chain of the homotrimer comprising the S protein must open to expose the RBD (Kirchdoerfer et al., 2016; Henderson et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2020; Sztain et al., 2021).
evidence: Description of S protein mechanism with citations.

claim: The binding of host cell protease Furin aids in the cleavage of the S protein into two domains: S1 and S2.
source: The Furin cleavage site plays a key role in the opening process as the binding of host cell protease Furin aids in the cleavage of the S protein into two domains: S1 and S2 (Wrobel et al., 2020: 13).
evidence: Description of Furin function with citation.
